lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
question: A 5-server cluster's leader is in term 3 with commitIndex 5. Its entries 6 to 9 all have term 3. The matchIndex values (leader included) are 9, 9, 8, 6, 5. What is the new commitIndex?
explain: Sorted descending: 9, 9, 8, 6, 5. The middle value 8 is stored on three servers (two with 9, one with 8), a majority of 5, and entry 8 has the current term. Index 9 is on only two servers. So commitIndex becomes 8, which also commits 6 and 7.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
question: You switch from 1024-token chunks to 256-token chunks and keep top-k at 2. What is the most likely new problem?
options: Each chunk's embedding becomes vaguer, so precision drops
The prompt overflows the context window
The LLM now sees a quarter as much text, so answers that span several sentences may lose a needed piece
Overlap stops working because it only applies to large chunks
explain: Smaller chunks give sharper embeddings, but 2 chunks of 256 tokens is 512 tokens of evidence instead of 2048. That is why the LlamaIndex example doubles top-k when it halves chunk size. Our toy shows the same thing: with 12-word chunks the 6 weeks chunk sits at rank 4.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: The seven failure points and how to debug them
question: A user asks for the refund policy as a bulleted list. The answer is correct and grounded but comes back as one paragraph. Which failure point is this?
options: FP 5 Wrong Format
FP 4 Not Extracted
FP 7 Incomplete
FP 2 Missed the Top Ranked Documents
explain: The facts are present and right; only the requested format was ignored. Barnett et al. define FP 5 as the LLM ignoring an instruction to extract information in a certain format such as a table or list.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
question: Which feature is most likely to be inflated by position bias?
options: Title BM25
Query-URL click count
URL length
Document age
explain: Click counts depend on where the document was shown: top results get examined and clicked more even when a lower result is more relevant, as the swapped-order experiment showed. The other three do not depend on past rankings.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: nDCG precisely: gain, discount, log base and the ideal
question: A run's grade 3 document at rank 1 and grade 1 document at rank 4 swap places. Which raw DCG@5 variant drops more?
options: Linear gain, because it is proportional to the grade
Neither, because DCG ignores grades beyond binary relevance
Exponential gain, because it makes the grade 3 worth 7 instead of 3
They drop equally, because only the discounts change
explain: The swap costs (gain difference) x (1 - 0.431), where 1 and 0.431 are the discounts of ranks 1 and 4 (0.431 is 1 / log2 5). Linear gain: 2 x 0.569 = 1.14. Exponential gain: (7 - 1) x 0.569 = 3.41. Exponential gain amplifies anything involving the top grade, which is why it is preferred when a few excellent results matter most.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
question: You compare 8 rankers pairwise with 28 independent paired t-tests at alpha = 0.05 and find 2 significant differences. What is the main concern?
options: With 28 tests, the chance of at least one false positive is about 0.76, so 2 hits are weak evidence; use ANOVA plus a multiple comparison test such as randomised Tukey HSD
The t-test cannot be used with paired data
The Wilcoxon test would have been more accurate
Nothing; each test is valid on its own
explain: 1 - 0.95^28 is about 0.76, so finding a couple of significant pairs is close to what chance alone would produce. Sakai suggests testing all systems together first and then applying a multiple comparison procedure. Smucker et al. found Wilcoxon less reliable, not more.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The way in: brokers, stolen logins and edge devices
question: A help desk agent resets MFA for a caller who knows the employee's name, ID and manager. Which control from the script closes this route?
options: MFA everywhere
Patching KEV vulnerabilities
Killing VPN sessions
Strong caller verification at the help desk
explain: The route does not attack the login technology; it asks a person to issue a new factor. Only a verification process that an attacker with public or stolen facts cannot pass (for example a call-back to a number on file, or approval by the manager) closes it.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Inside a crew: what the Conti playbook taught defenders
question: Why does the hunt escalate SRV-FILE-1 but only review SRV-APP-4?
options: SRV-FILE-1 is a file server and those are always critical
SRV-FILE-1 shows three different stages of the playbook in a few hours; SRV-APP-4 shows one tool
GMER is less dangerous than AdFind
SRV-APP-4 is on the allowlist
explain: Combining stages raises confidence, as correlation rules in the logging course did: discovery, persistence and exfiltration together form the attack chain. A single tool may be explainable; it is still reviewed, not ignored.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Recovery sequencing: identity first, then the business
question: Microsoft recommends restoring AD from a backup taken a few days before the failure rather than the latest one. Why?
options: The most recent backup may contain the attacker's changes, so a slightly older one trades some lost data for a lower risk of reintroducing them
Older backups are smaller
Recent backups cannot be restored on new hardware
Tombstone lifetime forbids recent backups
explain: The guide calls it a trade-off between recency and safety. Changes after the backup are lost, but a backup from inside the compromise window can bring back backdoor accounts and permissions.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
question: A cache server registers each 4 KB request buffer just before using it and deregisters it after. Throughput is poor. What is the best fix?
options: Use RDMA READ instead of WRITE
Register one large pool at startup, preferably on huge pages, and reuse buffers from it
Disable the protection domain
Use more QPs
explain: Registration enters the kernel and pins pages, so per-request registration puts the slow control path back on the data path. Registering a pool once fixes that, and large pages keep the NIC's translation cache small (FaRM's lesson).

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
question: Your RC QP has `timeout = 14` and `retry_cnt = 7`. A peer machine loses power mid-transfer. What does the sender see, and roughly when?
options: Nothing; the WR stays pending forever
An IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR completion after on the order of half a second, with the QP in an error state
An RNR error immediately
A TCP reset
explain: With no ACKs, the NIC retries after each 67.1 ms timeout; once retry_cnt is exhausted the WR completes with IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR (about 8 x 67 ms = 537 ms in the simple model). RNR is about missing receive buffers on a live peer, not a dead one.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
question: A Colyseus room has 200 entities and you call `sort()` on their ArraySchema every tick to keep a leaderboard ordered. Bandwidth spikes. Why?
options: Sorting changes refIds, which forces a full resync
Schemas cannot hold more than 63 entities
sort() marks every index as changed, so the whole array is re-sent every patch
Sorted arrays disable delta encoding for the whole room
explain: The Colyseus optimization docs: sort() re-sends every element because every index is marked changed. Sort a plain copy on the client, or sort a separate array of indexes, instead.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
question: Why does the identity Y transpose C Y = Y transpose Y + Y transpose (C - I) Y, with C user u's diagonal confidence matrix, matter?
options: It makes the loss convex in X and Y jointly
It lets each user update cost depend on that user's n_u touched items instead of all n items, so a sweep is linear in the number of non-zeros
It removes the need for regularization
It turns ALS into SGD
explain: Y transpose Y is shared and precomputed once per sweep. The user-specific correction only involves rows with c_ui different from 1, which are the items the user touched.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
question: When is a single pixels-per-mm ratio from the card exact for an object on the same table?
options: Whenever the card and the object are both fully visible
When you average the ratios from all four edges
When the image plane is parallel to the table, so every table point has the same depth
When the object is shorter than the card
explain: With the camera looking straight at the plane, every point on it has the same Z, so f/Z is one constant. Averaging edges or keeping the object short reduces nothing about perspective; only a fronto-parallel view (image plane parallel to the table) makes the ratio constant (ignoring lens distortion).

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
question: Which input should a hash join normally build its hash table on?
options: The larger input, so probing is cheaper
Whichever comes first in the FROM clause
The input that is already sorted
The smaller input, so the table fits in memory
explain: Build cost and memory grow with the build side, while each probe is a constant-time lookup either way. Building on the smaller input keeps the table in memory and avoids batching. In the docs' plan the Hash node sits over the 100-row tenk1 scan, not the 10000-row tenk2.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
question: N = 5 with R = 4, W = 2. Reads always overlap the last write, yet two clients writing the same key at the same time can both succeed without either write reaching a replica that has the other. Why?
options: Because R + W = 6 is too close to N
Because W = 2 is not a majority of 5, so two write sets can be disjoint
Because reads with R = 4 cannot tolerate failures
Because coordinators send writes to only W replicas
explain: Read/write overlap needs $R + W > N$. Write/write overlap needs $2W > N$. Two sets of 2 fit disjointly inside 5 replicas, so concurrent writers cannot detect each other through a shared replica.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
question: Which of these is NOT reward hacking?
options: An agent edits the unit tests so they pass without fixing the bug
A robot moves between the camera and the object so a learned reward model thinks it grasped it
A model fails a coding task because it cannot write the algorithm, and gets reward 0
A boat circles to re-collect shaping points instead of finishing the race
explain: Reward hacking requires a high proxy score with poor true performance. A model that honestly fails gets a low proxy score that matches its true performance: that is a capability gap, not a specification failure.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
question: Gao et al. found that a KL penalty in their PPO runs did not improve the gold score reached at a given KL. Which interpretation matches their paper?
options: KL penalties make overoptimization worse
KL penalties have no effect on training
The gold RM was itself hacked
The penalty acted like early stopping: it changed where training converged, not the gold-versus-KL frontier
explain: Gold scores depended only on the KL reached; the penalty made training converge earlier on the same frontier. They also caution the result may be sensitive to hyperparameters, and Coste et al. found a small KL penalty useful when combined with RM ensembles.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Catching hacks: CoT monitors, obfuscation, generalization
question: Your RL task family scores each episode pass or fail, capped at 1. Which of the detection signals in this lesson stops working there?
options: Inspecting anomalously high-scoring runs, since every pass scores the same 1
LLM monitors reading the transcript
Diff inspection of changed files
Hidden tests
explain: METR notes the high-score heuristic does not work for HCAST tasks for exactly this reason: with binary, capped scores a hack cannot score higher than an honest pass. They used an LLM monitor there instead. Diffs and hidden tests do not depend on the score's range.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
question: Why does the code draw a fresh TEF and vulnerability for every simulated year instead of fixing them once?
options: To make the program slower
Because PERT only works for one draw
Because the Poisson function requires it
Because the true values are uncertain, and drawing them each year spreads that uncertainty into the result
explain: The ranges express uncertainty about the inputs themselves. Sampling them per iteration propagates that uncertainty into the loss distribution; fixing them would understate the spread.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
question: During a Type II period, an engineer merges a hotfix without review under pressure during an outage. What should happen so the audit treats it correctly?
options: Delete the commit history
Nothing; auditors do not look at hotfixes
Follow the documented emergency change procedure: record the reason, get a retrospective review and approval soon after, and keep the ticket
Rewrite the change as a Type I control
explain: Emergency changes are normal; undocumented ones are exceptions. A defined emergency process with retrospective approval is a control the auditor can test.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: EU law for engineers: GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act
question: A database backup with customer emails is found on a public bucket. It was encrypted with a key stored only in your KMS, and access logs show no downloads of the key. Under GDPR Article 34, must you notify the affected individuals?
options: Yes, always within 72 hours
No, and you need not record it anywhere
Probably not: Art. 34(3)(a) exempts data rendered unintelligible to unauthorised people, such as by encryption; still document it and assess whether the authority must be told
Only if more than 500 people are affected
explain: Encryption with an uncompromised key is the textbook Art. 34(3)(a) case. Art. 33(5) still requires documenting all breaches, and you assess risk for the Art. 33 authority notification.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
question: Your insurance application says 'MFA is enforced on all remote access'. A forgotten VPN appliance allows password-only logins, and ransomware enters through it. What is the risk?
options: None; insurance always pays
The deductible doubles automatically
The insurer may dispute or deny the claim because the declared control was not in place
Only the VPN vendor is liable
explain: The NCSC warns that if you claim measures are in place when they are not, the insurer may not be obliged to pay. Applications deserve the same accuracy as audit evidence.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
question: In the memory example, offloading the training state raised KV capacity from about 44 to 60 full-length sequences per GPU. Why does that speed up rollout rather than just saving memory?
options: Offloading makes each decode step use FP32, which is more accurate
A larger KV cache lets each engine decode more sequences per step, and decode steps cost nearly the same at larger batch, so tokens per second rise
The KV cache stores model weights, so a larger cache means fewer weight reads
It removes the need for weight sync
explain: Decode is memory-bandwidth bound: each step reads all the weights whatever the batch size, so packing more sequences into a step raises tokens per second. The KV cache limits how many sequences fit, so freeing memory for it raises rollout throughput.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: The roofline: attainable FLOP/s versus intensity
question: A vendor releases a GPU with twice the Tensor Core FLOP/s of its predecessor and the same memory bandwidth. Which kernel speeds up the most?
options: A batch 1 GEMV at 1 FLOP/byte
A large square GEMM at about 1,365 FLOP/byte
A softmax at about 1 FLOP/byte
All three speed up by the same 2x
explain: Doubling the flat roof only raises kernels to the right of the old ridge. The GEMV and softmax sit on the sloped bandwidth line, which did not move, so they gain nothing. Only the high intensity GEMM can climb to the new, higher roof.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
question: Your service map has no edge between cart and catalog, yet during an incident both are anomalous and both are on the frontier. What is the most likely explanation worth checking first?
options: A hidden shared dependency (same hosts, same cache, same config push) that is not drawn in the map
Two independent faults at the same moment
The frontier rule does not apply to services with multiple callers
Granger causality between the two metric streams
explain: Two simultaneous frontier nodes usually mean one missing edge, not two faults. Shared infrastructure is the common culprit, and checking it is cheap: look for a resource, host set, or recent change the two have in common. Two genuinely independent faults do happen, but they are the less likely hypothesis, and the troubleshooting chapter's advice applies: when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
question: Why do D1 and D3 tie exactly in the toy example?
options: Rounding to two decimals hides the difference
RRF gives every document that appears in two lists the same score
Their rank pairs (1, 3) and (3, 1) contain the same ranks, and RRF sums the same terms in a different order
Both have the same BM25 score
explain: RRF depends only on the multiset of a document's ranks: the ranks it received, counted with repeats, ignoring which list gave which. 1/61 + 1/63 equals 1/63 + 1/61. D2 is also in two lists but with ranks (2, 5), so it scores lower: two-list documents are not all equal.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Build, load and test a Rust module
question: `CONFIG_RUST` does not appear anywhere in `make LLVM=1 menuconfig`, although `rustc` is installed. What is the right first step?
options: Add `CONFIG_RUST=y` to `.config` by hand and rebuild
Rebuild the kernel with GCC instead of LLVM
Enable `SAMPLES_RUST` first, which makes `CONFIG_RUST` visible
Run `make LLVM=1 rustavailable`, which runs Kconfig's availability check and prints what is missing
explain: The option is shown only when RUST_IS_AVAILABLE is true. Editing .config by hand does not help: the next olddefconfig drops an option whose dependencies fail. GCC support is very experimental, and SAMPLES_RUST itself depends on RUST. rustavailable explains the failure, for example a missing rust-src component or a bindgen that cannot find libclang.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Pinning: building kernel objects where they will live
question: Which struct field must be declared with `#[pin]` and initialized with `<-`?
options: `count: u64`
`name: &'static CStr`
`state: Mutex<State>`
`buf: KVec<u8>` (the vector's heap buffer may be reallocated)
explain: The `Mutex` wraps a C `struct mutex` that the kernel requires to stay at the address it was initialized at, so it is pinned and built in place with `new_mutex!`. A `KVec` may move its *buffer* on growth, but the KVec struct itself (pointer, length, capacity) can be moved freely.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Real device drivers: probe, remove, Devres and Revocable
question: Where should the PCI sample put a final register write that tells the device to stop?
options: In `Drop for SampleDriverData`, after the Bar has been dropped
In `unbind`, which runs while the device is still bound and the BAR is mapped
In `probe`, before returning the data
In `post_unbind_rust`, which drivers implement themselves
explain: The pci::Driver docs say unbind is for teardown that needs the device, such as I/O; resource release belongs in Drop. Fields are dropped after Drop::drop returns, so the Bar is still mapped inside Drop's body too, but unbind is the documented place and it also receives the &Device<Core> needed for bus-specific calls. post_unbind_rust is the adapter's internal callback, not a driver method.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
question: Your scheduler's select_cpu always returns CPU 0 for every task but never inserts anything. Your enqueue puts every task in one shared custom DSQ, and dispatch moves from it. Where do tasks actually run?
options: On whichever CPU calls dispatch and moves them to its local DSQ, so across all CPUs
Only on CPU 0, because select_cpu pins the task there
On CPU 0 for the first slice, then anywhere
The core rejects the scheduler for returning the same CPU every time
explain: select_cpu's return value is a non-binding hint (and the CPU it wakes if idle). Without an insertion there, the task goes through enqueue into the shared DSQ, and any CPU running dispatch can move it to its own local DSQ.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
question: Why does scx_rusty's dispatch try its own domain's DSQ before stealing from another LLC's?
options: The kernel forbids moving a task between LLCs
Stealing is reserved for the user-space balancer
Domain DSQs are FIFO while others are vtime ordered
Its own domain's tasks most likely still have data in this L3, so they start warm
explain: Every CPU in a domain shares one L3. A task queued there probably ran there recently. Stealing balances load at the price of a cold cache, so rusty does it only when its own queue is empty.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Secrets: what they are, how long they live, why they sprawl
question: A key is leaked and nobody ever notices. Which change most reduces how long an attacker can use it?
options: Making the key longer (512 bits instead of 256)
Storing it base64-encoded
Moving the repository from public to private
Giving it a short lifetime so it expires on its own
explain: With no detection, the usable window is limited only by the key's remaining life (L/2 on average). Key length defends against guessing, not theft; base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse; a private repository still leaks to everyone with access, and copies already taken stay valid.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Vaults: one place to store, control and audit secrets
question: A Vault cluster with the default Shamir seal reboots at 03:00 after a power cut. What happens to applications that read secrets from it?
options: Nothing: Vault unseals itself from its disk
They keep working from Vault's cache
Vault falls back to plaintext mode
Their reads fail until three share holders submit their shares
explain: A Shamir-sealed Vault forgets its root key on restart and waits for a quorum of humans. That is the security property and also the availability cost, which is why many deployments use auto unseal with a KMS or HSM.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Binding and auditing every decrypt: encryption context and transit
question: What does adding `{"tenant": "alice"}` as encryption context protect against?
options: Someone reading the context from the logs
Brute-forcing the KMS key
Replay of network traffic to KMS
A ciphertext or wrapped key being moved to another record and decrypted in the wrong place
explain: The context is bound to the ciphertext as authenticated data, so decrypting it under a different context fails. It is deliberately not secret (it is logged in plaintext), and it does nothing about key strength or network replay.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and a signing key that should have died in 2021
question: Microsoft's September 2023 blog said the key most probably leaked through a crash dump. What does the CSRB report say about that?
options: It confirmed the crash dump with logs
The key was brute-forced
An insider was identified
Microsoft found no crash dump containing the key, corrected the blog in March 2024, and still does not know how the key was obtained
explain: The Board found no evidence for the crash dump theory and criticised the delay in correcting it. The lesson for responders: say what you know, label hypotheses as hypotheses, and correct public statements quickly.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: archives, asserts, temp files and what Bandit sees
question: A deployment runs `python -O app.py`. Which check in the code silently stops working?
options: `assert user.is_admin`
`if not user.is_admin: abort(403)`
`hmac.compare_digest(a, b)`
`tarfile.extractall(d, filter='data')`
explain: With -O, __debug__ is False and assert statements are compiled away. The if/abort, compare_digest and the extraction filter are ordinary code and still run.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Go: nil maps, data races and the race detector
question: A team's tests pass under `go test -race` with no reports. Can they conclude the code is race-free?
options: No, it only reports races on paths the tests actually executed
Yes, the detector checks all code statically
Yes, as long as the tests ran twice
No, because the race detector only works on maps
explain: The Go documentation says the detector finds only races that happen at run time, so unexecuted paths are invisible. It is not a static analyser, and it detects races on any memory, not just maps.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: C review checklist: strings, sizes and return values
question: Which line has the bug a reviewer should flag?
options: `void g(char d[32]) { memcpy(d, s, sizeof(d)); }`
`void f(char *d, size_t cap) { snprintf(d, cap, "%s", s); }`
`char b[32]; fgets(b, sizeof b, stdin);`
`p = calloc(count, sizeof *p); if (!p) return -1;`
explain: A parameter written as char d[32] is still a pointer, so sizeof(d) is 8, not 32: the copy length is wrong (and clang's -Wsizeof-array-argument warns). The other lines take the size from the real buffer or check the result.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Memory-safe roadmaps: CISA's guidance and Android's numbers
question: A team proposes a new TLS certificate parser in C for a network appliance. Based on CISA's Bad Practices guidance, what is the strongest review question?
options: Why is a new network-facing component being written in a memory-unsafe language when memory-safe alternatives exist, and what is the roadmap?
Is the code formatted with the house style?
Has the parser been benchmarked against OpenSSL?
Does the parser have a README?
explain: The guidance calls new product development in memory-unsafe languages dangerous where alternatives exist, and asks roadmaps to prioritise network-facing code. A parser of untrusted network input is exactly the case it describes.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec building blocks: SAs, SPIs, ESP, AH and two modes
question: A site wants integrity protection only, without encryption, for traffic that crosses a NAT router. What does NIST SP 800-77 recommend?
options: AH in tunnel mode, because AH is designed for integrity
AH plus ESP with NULL encryption, for two layers of integrity
No IPsec, because integrity without encryption is pointless
ESP with NULL encryption and an integrity algorithm, or ESP with AES-GMAC
explain: NIST discourages AH and recommends ESP with NULL encryption (plus an integrity algorithm) or AES-GMAC when encryption is not wanted. ESP's integrity check does not cover the outer IP header, so the NAT rewriting addresses does not break it. AH+ESP combined mode is no longer recommended.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: WireGuard: one interface, public keys and cryptokey routing
question: Why does WireGuard have no algorithm negotiation?
options: To make the handshake fit in one UDP packet
Because ChaCha20 can never be broken
Because the Linux kernel supports only one cipher
To remove the complexity and downgrade risk of cipher agility; if a primitive breaks, all endpoints upgrade
explain: The paper calls WireGuard "cryptographically opinionated" and says cipher agility "increases complexity monumentally", citing the long run of SSL/TLS vulnerabilities. The cost is that a broken primitive means a new protocol version for everyone.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: RADIUS and TACACS+: central logins for network devices
question: An attacker on the network between a switch and its RADIUS server captures an Access-Request. Without the shared secret, what can they read?
options: Nothing, RADIUS packets are encrypted
The User-Name and other attributes in clear, but not the password, which is XORed with an MD5 of the secret
Only the password, because RADIUS encrypts everything else
Everything, because RADIUS sends the shared secret in the packet
explain: RADIUS hides only the User-Password attribute. User names, NAS address and port, and every reply attribute travel in the clear. The secret itself never travels in a packet.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Encrypting email itself: S/MIME, OpenPGP and EFAIL (2018)
question: DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) and DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) let a receiver check that an email really comes from the domain it names. Why does a valid DKIM or DMARC result not protect against EFAIL?
options: Because the attacker sends the altered ciphertext in a new email from their own domain, which can pass DKIM and DMARC for that domain
Because DKIM uses MD5
Because DMARC only applies to S/MIME, not OpenPGP
It does protect: EFAIL emails always fail DMARC
explain: DKIM and DMARC authenticate the sending domain, not the encrypted content. The EFAIL FAQ: the attacker copies the ciphertext into a new message sent under their own name with valid SPF (Sender Policy Framework, which lists the servers allowed to send for a domain), DKIM and DMARC.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Bell-LaPadula: no read up, no write down
question: Under Bell-LaPadula, a subject labelled (SECRET, {NUCLEAR}) asks for an object labelled (SECRET, {CRYPTO}). What is allowed?
options: Read only, because the levels are equal
Write only, because writing across equal levels is safe
Both, because the levels are equal
Neither, because neither label dominates the other
explain: Dominance needs both the level and the categories. Neither category set contains the other, so neither label dominates: read fails the simple security property and write fails the star property.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Assurance: the Orange Book, Common Criteria and what they prove
question: Under the 2014 CCRA, what is mutually recognised across member countries?
options: Any certificate at any EAL
Only EAL7 certificates
Certificates up to EAL2 plus flaw remediation, or those based on collaborative protection profiles
Only certificates issued by the US
explain: The arrangement limits recognition to components up to EAL2 and ALC_FLR (flaw remediation), or to cPP-based evaluations with assurance activities up to EAL4. Higher levels may be valid nationally but carry a note that CCRA recognition is limited.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The trust algorithm: criteria, scores and context
question: Why does SP 800-207 warn about a tuning phase?
options: Because trust algorithms need training data before they work at all
Because new criteria and weights will wrongly deny some legitimate requests until they are adjusted to real workflows
Because policy engines are slow at first
Because the law requires a pilot
explain: Policies written from documents rarely match how people actually work. Expect false denials and adjust, the same lesson as BeyondCorp's logging mode, while measuring how many wrong decisions the business will tolerate.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: SASE, SSE and the cloud edge: SD-WAN, SWG, CASB and FWaaS
question: A vendor sells SWG, CASB and ZTNA from its cloud, but no SD-WAN or WAN optimisation. Which term fits best?
options: SASE
SSE
FWaaS
NGFW
explain: SSE is the security service set without the WAN networking half; adding SD-WAN makes it SASE. FWaaS is a single function, and an NGFW (next-generation firewall) is usually an appliance.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Webhooks: accepting only events you can trust
question: Why compare signatures with hmac.compare_digest rather than ==?
options: == can stop at the first differing character, so response timing can reveal how much of a guessed signature is correct
== is too slow for hex strings
compare_digest also checks the timestamp
== does not work on strings with a sha256= prefix
explain: Early exit leaks information through time. compare_digest avoids content-based short-circuiting. It does not check timestamps: replay protection is a separate step.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Case management APIs, and reading Netflix's Dispatch
question: Why do Dispatch's canary signals skip deduplication?
options: Canaries are always malicious
Deduplication is too slow for them
Each synthetic test signal must travel the whole ingest path on its own, rather than being folded into an earlier instance, so it proves the pipeline works
Canaries create cases that must not be merged
explain: A canary's job is to show the path works end to end. Folding it into a previous result would hide a broken pipeline. In Dispatch's code canaries are stored without creating a case at all, so nobody is paged.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Measuring AI triage: golden sets, precision, recall and attack success
question: A new prompt scores TP 19, FN 1, FP 60, TN 120 on the same 200 alerts. Compared with the old prompt (precision 0.36, recall 0.85), what changed?
options: Recall rose to 0.95 while precision fell to 0.24: fewer missed attacks, more benign escalations
Both precision and recall improved
Recall fell and precision rose
Nothing measurable changed
explain: Recall = 19/20 = 0.95. Precision = 19/(19+60) = 0.24. Missing one attack instead of three is usually worth thirty more benign escalations, but the team should make that trade knowingly.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
question: A researcher publishes code that shows a router bug can be triggered, but nobody has used it against anyone. Which word fits that code best?
options: A threat source
A payload already in the wild
A risk
A proof-of-concept exploit
explain: Code that demonstrates a vulnerability can be exploited is a proof of concept (PoC). It is not yet active exploitation: CISA says PoC code and security research do not count as exploitation in the wild. The threat source is a person or group, and risk is an assessment, not code.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Scoring and prioritising: CVSS, KEV and EPSS
question: A vector changes from UI:N to UI:R (a user must click something). With everything else the same, what happens to the base score?
options: It goes up, because users are unreliable
It stays the same, because UI is an impact metric
It drops to 0
It goes down, because the exploitability term shrinks (0.85 becomes 0.62)
explain: UI is an exploitability metric. Required interaction makes the attack harder, so the multiplier falls from 0.85 to 0.62 and the base score drops. Impact is unchanged.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Defence in depth: layers, and why they must be independent
question: Three layers each stop 90% of attacks, independently. What fraction of attacks get through all three?
explain: Each layer lets 10% through, and independence means the fractions multiply: 0.1 x 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.001, which is 0.1%.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
question: Why is passive voice especially harmful in a security recommendation?
options: It is grammatically wrong
It makes sentences too short
It hides who must act, and ownership is usually the thing that decides whether a fix happens
Executives do not understand passive voice
explain: Plain language guidance notes that passive voice obscures who handles what. In remediation, an action with no named actor is the Equifax failure in miniature.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
question: A summary lists 23 findings by severity and stops. What is it missing most?
options: A longer methodology section
Screenshots
A verdict and an ask: what the numbers mean for the decision at hand, and what the reader must decide, by when
The CVSS vectors
explain: Counts without a conclusion leave the decision-maker to do the analysis. The summary's job is to answer their question and state the decision needed.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Design-review and code-review comments that get acted on
question: You are not sure a pattern in a PR is exploitable. What is the best comment?
options: Block the merge until the author proves it is safe
Say nothing
A question: explain the concern and ask whether this input can ever come from a user, marked non-blocking unless the answer is yes
Mark it as an issue and Critical to be safe
explain: Questions are for uncertain concerns. Blocking on a guess burns trust; silence risks missing a bug. A clear question gets the author's knowledge on the record.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
question: After three rounds in the toy, move d has prior 0. Suppose d was actually the best move and its value estimate was wrong. What happens in later rounds without exploration noise?
options: d is never visited, because its exploration bonus is P(d) times something, which is 0, and its Q stays 0
800 simulations are enough that the search reaches d eventually
The value loss on z will raise P(d) automatically
The gate at 55% will reject the network and restore d
explain: The pUCT bonus is proportional to the prior. With P(d) = 0 and an unvisited Q of 0, d never has the highest score, so the search never looks at it and the outcome z never reflects it. This is exactly why AlphaZero adds Dirichlet noise to the root prior during self-play.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
question: In ReST, reward model scores keep rising with every Grow step, but human raters prefer the model after one Grow step. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The policy is increasingly exploiting errors in the learned reward model, a proxy for human judgment
Human raters are noisier than the reward model, so their results should be ignored
The Improve thresholds were set too low
Translation quality cannot improve after one Grow step for any method
explain: The reward model is only a proxy. Optimizing a proxy harder eventually finds outputs it overrates. The ReST authors say exactly this and suggest periodically refreshing the reward model with human labels on the newest policy's outputs.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof
question: SPIRAL trains one policy for both seats of TicTacToe with REINFORCE. Why does a single global baseline give misleading advantages?
options: The two seats have different expected returns (first-move advantage), so a global baseline credits the seat instead of the moves
A global baseline has higher variance only for single-player games
REINFORCE cannot use any baseline in multi-agent settings
The global baseline makes the game no longer zero-sum
explain: If the first player wins more often, a global baseline makes nearly every first-player move look good and every second-player move look bad. RAE subtracts a separate running mean per game and seat, so only better-than-usual play for that seat is reinforced.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
question: You add the user's name and the current time to the very top of the system prompt to personalize replies. What happens to the two caches?
options: Prompt caching stops working because the prefix now differs per request; the semantic cache is unaffected if it embeds only the user's question
Both stop working
Neither is affected
The semantic cache stops working; prompt caching is unaffected
explain: Prefix matching is exact from the first token, so a per-request value at the top breaks every reuse. Put stable content first and variable content last. A semantic cache keyed on the user's question does not see the system prompt, which is exactly why it needs scoping when the system prompt matters.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: IMDSv2: session tokens, PUT and a hop limit of 1
question: An attacker has remote code execution on an EC2 instance that requires IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1. Can they read the role credentials?
options: No: the token requirement blocks them
No: the TTL of 1 drops the token
Only if the instance has a public IP address
Yes: code on the instance can send its own PUT, receive the token directly and use it
explain: IMDSv2 protects against requests relayed by something else (WAFs, proxies, SSRF, routers). Code running on the instance is exactly the legitimate client IMDS is built to serve. That is why role permissions must still follow least privilege.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Insecure deserialization: when loading data runs code
question: A Java service checks `if (!(obj instanceof Cart)) throw ...` right after `readObject()`. Why does this not stop a gadget chain?
options: instanceof is slow
The chain runs inside readObject, while the object graph is being built, before the check executes
Gadget chains only affect PHP
Cart must implement Externalizable
explain: Deserialization hooks run as each object is reconstructed. By the time readObject returns and your check runs, any side effect has already happened. Filters must act before construction, which is what ObjectInputFilter does.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
question: What is the strongest design for a "download your invoice" endpoint?
options: Accept a file name and strip every dot and slash
Accept an invoice ID, check the user owns it, look up the stored path server-side, and never put user text in a path
Accept a full path but only allow paths ending in .pdf
Accept a file name and URL-decode it twice before checking
explain: If user input never reaches the filesystem API, there is nothing to traverse, and the ownership check also closes the IDOR hole from the access-control course. Extension checks and character stripping are both known to be bypassable.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
question: Why does the interpreter send the shared prefix to the runtime before the fork branches?
options: So that the prefix is computed and inserted into the radix tree once; branches arriving together would otherwise each find nothing cached and each prefill it
Because the runtime cannot accept prompts longer than the prefix
To let the runtime pick a different model for each branch
Because RadixAttention only works when requests arrive one at a time
explain: If both branches arrive at the same moment with nothing cached, each matches zero tokens and each computes the shared part. The paper calls the fix a frontend hint: it simplifies runtime matching and is one of the co-design benefits in its ablation.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
question: In the toy graph, a planner picks the route with the fewest roads and breaks ties arbitrarily. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; fewest roads always means fastest when weights are minutes
It may return S, C, F, T (14 min) even though S, D, F, T takes 9 min
It cannot find any route, because BFS ignores weights entirely
It always returns the slowest 3-road route
explain: Three routes tie at 3 roads (9, 10 and 14 minutes). Hop count ignores weights, so any of them can come out. We need an algorithm that compares accumulated minutes, which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm does.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: A travel time function says: leave at 08:05 and arrive at 08:30.6, or leave at 08:10 and arrive at 08:27.4. What does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: Admissibility; A* would overestimate
Nonnegative weights; travel times went negative
FIFO; waiting would beat leaving now, which breaks the label-setting search for earliest arrival
Turn restrictions; the profile is missing a penalty
explain: Leaving later and arriving earlier violates FIFO. Then arriving at a node as early as possible no longer guarantees arriving as early as possible further along, so a settled earliest-arrival label can be wrong. Dijkstra-style time-dependent search assumes FIFO, and the survey notes that other settings are studied separately.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
question: A drone's control loop needs a filtered gyro reading every 1 ms. Someone proposes `sosfiltfilt` because it has zero phase delay. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; zero phase is ideal for control
sosfiltfilt only works on FIR filters
sosfiltfilt runs the filter backward from the end of the signal, so it needs future samples and cannot run in real time
sosfiltfilt halves the filter order, so it filters too weakly
explain: The backward pass starts from the last sample, which a real-time loop does not have yet. Real-time systems must use a causal filter (sosfilt, or an FIR) and accept or compensate its delay. Forward-backward filtering doubles the effective order; it does not halve it.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
question: In AVX-512, `r = _mm512_mask_add_ps(src, k, a, b)` with k = 0x0003. What are lanes 0 and 5 of r?
options: Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = 0
Lane 0 = src0, lane 5 = a5 + b5
Both lanes are a + b; k only affects stores
Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = src5
explain: 0x0003 sets bits 0 and 1, so lanes 0 and 1 get a + b. The mask_ form is merge masking: inactive lanes copy src. The maskz_ form would have produced 0 in lane 5.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
question: Why does a program not simply call `mmap` for every 24-byte object?
options: mmap cannot return memory smaller than a page, and each call is a system call, so it is both wasteful and slow
mmap memory cannot be written to until it is passed through malloc
mmap always returns memory on a different NUMA node
mmap regions are freed automatically after one function returns
explain: mmap works in whole pages (4 KiB on typical x86-64) and costs a kernel entry per call. An allocator amortizes both costs by carving many small objects out of one mapping. (A NUMA node, a group of CPUs with its own local memory on a non-uniform memory access machine, has nothing to do with it.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
question: You want to raise SGLang's KV cache budget inside a slime run. SGLang's own flag is `--mem-fraction-static`. What do you pass to slime's train.py?
options: `--sglang-mem-fraction-static 0.8`
`--mem-fraction-static 0.8`, since slime forwards unknown flags
Nothing: slime fixes SGLang memory internally
`--rollout-mem-fraction 0.8`
explain: SGLang arguments are passed through with a `--sglang-` prefix. Unprefixed flags are interpreted as Megatron or slime arguments, and there is no slime-specific rollout memory flag.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
question: A teammate enables fully async rollout on a colocated 8-GPU job and sees no speedup. Why?
options: Fully async only works with PPO
The default --sglang-server-concurrency is too low
With colocation rollout and training share GPUs and must take turns, so there are no independent resources to overlap
Fully async requires delta weight sync
explain: The docs say fully async needs separate GPUs for meaningful overlap. On shared GPUs the phases still alternate, so the async bound does not apply.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
question: A rule detects `vssadmin delete shadows`. It fires because the backup product deletes old shadow copies every night at 01:00, exactly as configured. What is the verdict, and what is the fix?
options: False positive; delete the rule
True positive; escalate to incident response
Benign true positive; record the backup schedule and add a narrow, documented exception for that product's signed process at that time
Undetermined; leave it open
explain: The rule saw exactly what it was built to see, so it is not a false positive. The activity is legitimate, so it is not an attack. The fix is context: a narrow exception tied to the backup product, not deleting a rule that catches ransomware precursors.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Malware on an endpoint: reading a process tree
question: Four parent and child pairs appear in today's EDR data. Which deserves the fastest look?
options: explorer.exe starting WINWORD.EXE
explorer.exe starting chrome.exe
explorer.exe starting Teams.exe
WINWORD.EXE starting powershell.exe -EncodedCommand
explain: The first three are a user launching ordinary applications from the desktop. A word processor launching an encoded PowerShell command is a classic sign of a malicious document.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When to escalate, and case notes someone else can act on
question: Which case-note summary lets an incident lead act fastest?
options: "Weird stuff on a laptop, see the logs"
"Malware alert. Ran some queries. Looks bad."
"FIN-LT-042 ran a malicious macro at 09:15 UTC; an unknown device signed in as the user at 09:41. Host isolated, sessions revoked. Need IR to scope the account's access."
A copy of the full raw logs with no summary
explain: It states what happened, when, to what, how sure, what is already done and what is needed. The others force the reader to redo the triage.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
question: A company forces monthly password changes. An audit finds many passwords on sticky notes. What does Adams and Sasse's study suggest is the main cause?
options: Employees are careless and need stricter penalties
Sticky notes are too easy to buy
The policy demands more memorisation than people can manage, so they write passwords down to cope
Monthly changes are too infrequent
explain: Their respondents linked writing passwords down directly to forced changes and to having many passwords. Penalties do not reduce the memory load; changing the policy does.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
question: A caller claiming to be from IT gives a callback number 'in case we get cut off'. What should the employee do to verify the caller?
options: Call the number given, since that proves the caller answers it
Ask the caller three questions only real IT staff would know
Look up the service desk in the company directory and call that number instead
Check that caller ID shows the company's name
explain: A number supplied by the caller leads back to the caller. Caller ID and display names are set by the caller too. Only a number from a source the caller does not control, such as the directory, verifies anything.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Designing help-desk verification that holds under pressure
question: Which change most reduces the number of risky judgement calls the help desk has to make at all?
options: Longer calls with more personal questions
Self-service recovery that requires an existing strong factor, such as a passkey
Allowing resets by email
Publishing the help desk's verification questions
explain: If most people can recover by proving a factor they still hold, only the rare cases with no factor left reach an agent, and those can get the slow, strong checks.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Badges, readers and tailgating
question: A log shows badge B22 exiting the lab at 08:50 with no entry by B22 that day. What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: The badge reader's clock is wrong
B22 cloned someone else's card
B22 followed someone into the lab without badging (tailgating or piggybacking)
B22 works from home
explain: An exit with no matching entry is the classic trace of tailgating. Confirm with CCTV and a conversation, and look at whether the door-held alarm fired around the time B22 must have entered.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
question: After a tailgater is spotted in a restricted area, what should be preserved first?
options: The visitor sign-in sheet only
Nothing, as the person has left
CCTV footage and badge logs, before they are overwritten
The door hardware
explain: Recordings and logs often roll over after a set period. They show who entered, when, and where they went, including near network ports and unlocked screens.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
question: You compare a 4,096-latent and a 65,536-latent SAE on the same layer. The smaller one has a 'Python code' latent; the larger has several latents for different Python contexts and none that matches it exactly. What does this indicate?
options: The larger SAE is broken
Feature splitting: the wider dictionary covers the same concept at finer resolution
The smaller SAE has dead latents
Python is not represented in the model
explain: This is the expected pattern from Towards Monosemanticity: wider dictionaries refine broad latents into families of more specific ones.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Where SAEs fall short: absorption, missing features and weak baselines
question: Your team must flag customer messages that mention cancelling, and has 2,000 labelled examples. Which first approach does the evidence in this lesson support?
options: Search the SAE for a 'cancellation' latent and threshold it, since SAE latents are the model's true units
Train a much wider SAE until a perfect cancellation latent appears
Use raw model outputs only; internal activations cannot be probed
Train a linear probe or a difference-in-means direction on the raw activations, and use SAE latents only if they measurably add to it
explain: With labels available, Kantamneni et al. and AxBench found supervised baselines on raw activations match or beat SAE latents, especially under distribution shift. Wider SAEs absorb more, and SAE latents are not canonical units.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
question: Two sensors sit 10 m apart and read 30 and 31. A third sensor equally far from the target, in another direction, reads 12. Compared with IDW, how will ordinary kriging weight them (assume a range of several km)?
options: Exactly like IDW, because the distances to the target are equal
It gives the pair all the weight because they agree with each other
It gives every sensor weight 1/3 regardless of position
It gives the close pair less weight each, treating them almost like one sensor, and the lone sensor relatively more
explain: The pair is nearly redundant: $\Gamma$ shows they are strongly correlated with each other, so kriging splits roughly one sensor's worth of weight between them. IDW only looks at distance to the target, so it counts the pair twice.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: Draft q = (0.7, 0.3) and target p = (0.4, 0.6) over two tokens {A, B}. The draft proposes A. What is the probability A is kept, and if not, what is sampled?
options: Kept with prob 0.4; otherwise sample from p
Kept with prob 4/7; otherwise output B with probability 1
Kept with prob 0.7; otherwise output B
Always kept, since A has nonzero target probability
explain: Acceptance is min(1, p(A)/q(A)) = 0.4/0.7 = 4/7. The residual max(0, p - q) = (0, 0.3) normalizes to B with probability 1. Check: P(A) = 0.7 x 4/7 = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3 + 0.7 x 3/7 = 0.6.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
question: Which single change halves the number of spectrogram frames per second?
options: Increase the window from 25 ms to 50 ms
Increase the hop from 10 ms to 20 ms
Reduce the mel bands from 80 to 40
Resample from 16 kHz to 8 kHz but keep a 25 ms window and 10 ms hop
explain: Frames per second is 1 / hop, so a 20 ms hop gives 50 frames per second. A longer window makes each frame cover more time but they still start every 10 ms. Fewer mel bands makes each column shorter, not the sequence. Resampling changes samples per frame, not frames per second.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
question: A clinic transcribes hour-long recordings with long pauses, and reviewers find invented sentences in the quiet parts. Which change targets the cause most directly?
options: Use a larger beam
Run VAD and send only detected speech to the model
Lower the compression-ratio threshold to 1.5
Switch WER normalizers
explain: The invented text appears where there is no speech for the decoder to follow. Removing non-speech before decoding takes away the empty input the decoder fills. A larger beam or a stricter compression threshold targets loops, not fluent inventions, and a normalizer only changes scoring.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
question: A random-access hash table grows from 2 MiB to 512 MiB and slows down more than its cache miss rate explains. Which change most directly targets the extra cost?
options: Use a TLB with twice as many entries
Switch from malloc to calloc
Increase RLIMIT_STACK
Back the table with 2 MiB huge pages (for example madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE))
explain: 512 MiB of random access is far beyond a 4 KiB-page TLB's reach, so most accesses also need a page walk. 2 MiB pages raise reach 512 times, so the table needs only 256 translations. You cannot buy a bigger TLB in software, and the other options do not touch translation.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
question: What does ActAdd need in order to build a steering vector?
options: A labeled dataset of a few thousand examples and a few gradient steps
A trained linear probe on the target concept
One pair of contrasting prompts and two forward passes
Access to the model's training data
explain: ActAdd is optimization-free: two forward passes on a prompt pair such as Love and Hate, a subtraction, and a scale factor. CAA (lesson 2), ITI (inference-time intervention, developed independently of ActAdd, slightly earlier) and the reading vectors of RepE (representation engineering) use more examples to get a cleaner direction; none of these fine-tunes the model.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: Why is a random vector of the same norm a necessary baseline?
options: To check the hook is installed
Because random vectors are always better at steering
To show the effect comes from the direction and not from merely perturbing the stream by that much
To estimate the residual stream norm
explain: Any large perturbation changes outputs somewhat. ActAdd and ITI both compared against random directions (ITI's random direction moved TruthfulQA from 30.5% to only 31.2%) to show their direction specifically carries the concept.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: Your sink appends one row per window firing. With allowed lateness 5 s, window [0,10) fires at count 4 and later at count 5. A dashboard sums all rows per window. What goes wrong and what fixes it?
options: The window is counted as 4 + 5 = 9 readings; write with an upsert keyed by (sensor, window) since firings are accumulating
Nothing; the second firing contains only the late reading
Late firings are never sent to sinks
The fix is to set allowed lateness higher
explain: In accumulating mode each firing is the full refined result, so appending both rows double counts. Overwrite by window key, or use discarding mode and have the consumer add deltas, or emit retractions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
question: A bug report: a decoder trains to near-zero loss quickly, but generates garbage at inference. Which bug is most likely?
options: The scale factor uses d_model instead of d_k
The causal mask is missing, so during training each position could read the token it was supposed to predict
The model uses 8 heads instead of 1
The softmax is applied over columns instead of rows
explain: With teacher forcing the whole target is fed in at once. Without the causal mask, position i can attend to position i+1 (its own answer), so training is trivially easy. At inference those future tokens do not exist yet, and the model has never learned to predict without them.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
question: Which statement about beam search with beam size B = 1 is correct?
options: It is the same as greedy decoding: only the single best partial output is kept each step
It explores every possible sentence, so it always finds the most probable one
It needs teacher forcing at inference
It is the paper's setting for the base model
explain: Keeping one hypothesis and extending it by its most probable token is exactly greedy decoding. No practical beam search explores every sentence; the paper used B = 4. Teacher forcing applies only to training.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
question: Your index holds tweets whose lengths all fall between 25 and 35 tokens, and nothing else. You move b from 0.75 to 0.3. What do you expect?
options: Large ranking changes, because tweets vary in length
All scores become zero
Scores become probabilities
Small changes, because lengths are all close to avgdl so B stays near 1 either way
explain: B = (1 - b) + b x |d|/avgdl. When every |d|/avgdl is near 1, B is near 1 for any b, so b has little effect. b matters most when lengths vary a lot.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
question: In nanoGPT's Block, where is LayerNorm applied?
options: After each residual addition, x = LN(x + attn(x))
On the input to each sub-layer, x = x + attn(LN(x)), plus one final ln_f
Only once, before the first block
Only on the attention scores before the softmax
explain: GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the input of each sub-block and added a final LayerNorm after the last block. The first option is the post-LN layout of the 2017 Transformer.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: The training loop end to end: data, evals, overfitting, checkpoints
question: Why does nanoGPT store OpenWebText as uint16 and not int64 like the tensors it trains on?
options: Every GPT-2 token id is at most 50,256, which fits in 16 bits, so the 9-billion-token file is 4 times smaller; get_batch converts each slice to int64
uint16 makes the tokenizer faster
PyTorch embeddings require 16-bit indices
Negative ids mark document boundaries
explain: Two bytes per token gives the 17 GB train.bin; int64 would be 72 GB. The conversion to int64 happens only for the few slices that get_batch reads. End-of-text is the ordinary id 50256, not a negative number.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
question: Someone computes $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(x^2 + 1)$ at $x = 1$ and gets $1/2$. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; 1/2 is correct
They used 1/u with u = 2 but forgot to multiply by du/dx = 2x = 2; the answer is 1
They should have used 1/x, giving 1
The log has no derivative at 1
explain: Outer: $d\ln(u)/du = 1/u = 1/2$ at $u = 2$. Inner: $du/dx = 2x = 2$. The chain rule multiplies them: $1/2 \times 2 = 1$. Forgetting the inner factor is the most common chain-rule error.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
question: Two losses are $x^2 + 3y^2$ and $x^2 + 30y^2$. Compared with the first, what happens to the largest stable learning rate for plain gradient descent on the second?
options: It stays 1/3 because the x term is unchanged
It increases, because the bowl is steeper so it is easier to find the bottom
It drops to 1/30, because the steepest direction now has a = 30
It is unlimited, because the minimum is still at the origin
explain: Using the factor $1 - 2a\eta$, the $30y^2$ term needs $\eta < 1/30$. The steepest direction caps the step size for all parameters, so the shallow $x$ direction now crawls. This mismatch is called poor conditioning.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
question: A script `setup.sh` contains `cd build` and `export MODE=dev`. You run it as `./setup.sh`, then type `pwd`. What do you see?
options: Your original directory, and MODE is unset in your shell
The build directory, because the script changed into it
The build directory, but MODE is unset because export only affects children
An error, because cd is a builtin and cannot run in a script
explain: `./setup.sh` runs in a child bash process. Its cd and export change only that child, which then exits. To apply them to your current shell you must run the file inside it with `source setup.sh` (or `. setup.sh`).

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
question: `grep ERROR huge.log | head -n 5` returns almost instantly even though huge.log is 50 GB. Why?
options: grep detects the head command and reads only 5 lines
head reads the file directly and grep is skipped
The kernel caches the whole file before grep starts
Once head exits after 5 lines, grep's next write raises SIGPIPE and grep dies
explain: Both run concurrently. After head has its five lines it exits, closing the read end. grep's next write to the pipe triggers SIGPIPE, ending it long before it reaches the end of the file.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
question: Your public key is in the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, yet ssh falls back to asking for a password. On the server, `ls -ld ~/.ssh` shows `drwxrwxrwx`. What is the likely cause?
options: sshd will not use authorized_keys while ~/.ssh is writable by other users
The key type is wrong for this server
known_hosts on your laptop is missing
The private key must also be copied to the server
explain: Anyone who can write to `~/.ssh` could add their own key, so sshd refuses to trust authorized_keys there (its StrictModes check). `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` and `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys` fix it. The private key must never be copied to the server.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Train word2vec yourself: SGNS in PyTorch, then gensim
question: You change the PyTorch script to `torch.optim.Adam([v.weight, u.weight])` and keep `sparse=True`. What happens?
options: Training runs normally but uses more memory
Adam silently ignores the embedding rows
The first `opt.step()` raises an error, because Adam does not accept sparse gradients
Adam converts the gradients to dense and trains the same model
explain: PyTorch raises `RuntimeError: Adam does not support sparse gradients, please consider SparseAdam instead`. Either keep `sparse=True` with SparseAdam (or SGD), or drop `sparse=True` and use dense Adam, which then updates moment estimates for every row on every step.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Where word vectors fail: unseen words, many senses and bias
question: Your fastText model gives the unseen word *unhappiness* a vector close to *happiness* and *sadness*. Which part of the model made that possible?
options: The context vectors of the words around *unhappiness* at query time
A shared unknown-word row
The n-gram vectors it shares with seen words, such as *hap*, *ness* and *ness>*, summed into a vector
The full softmax over the vocabulary
explain: An unseen word has no word vector, but its character n-grams were trained inside other words. fastText sums their vectors. At query time there is no context and no training, and an unknown row would give every unseen word the same vector.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
question: Why does the GPU keep many warps resident on each SM?
options: So that while some warps wait for memory, others can execute math
Because each warp can only run one instruction in its lifetime
To increase the size of HBM
Because warps of 32 threads cannot share an SM
explain: GPUs hide dependent instruction and memory latency by switching to other ready warps. That is why the number of threads needed is much larger than the number of execution units.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
question: Which statement about running `./hello` is correct?
options: The shell reads hello's machine code and executes it itself
The CPU loads the ELF file from disk one instruction at a time as it runs
The kernel, via execve, replaces the current process image with hello and starts it at its entry point
The linker runs again every time you start the program
explain: execve(2): the program currently run by the calling process is replaced with a new one, with a newly initialized stack, heap and data segments. The CPU never reads from the disk file directly; pages of the file are mapped into memory and loaded when touched.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
question: A colleague's loop `for j: for i: total += m[i][j]` over a large C 2D array of longs is slow. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Swap the loops so the inner loop walks j along a row
Use a faster add instruction
Make total a global variable
Add more threads before changing anything
explain: In C, m[i][j] and m[i][j+1] are adjacent, so walking j in the inner loop uses all 8 longs of every 64-byte line it fetches. The current inner loop strides a full row per access, fetching a new line every time.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
question: A base model is given the prompt "Write a haiku about rain." Why might it fail to write a haiku?
options: It continues the text as a plausible document, which may be more instructions or a list of prompts rather than an answer
Its weights contain no knowledge of poetry, which only SFT adds
Base models cannot generate text without a reward model
The prompt is too short for the attention mechanism
explain: Pretraining optimizes next-token likelihood on documents. A line like this often appears in lists of writing prompts, so continuing with more prompts is a likely continuation. The knowledge of haiku is already in the base model; SFT and RLHF teach it to respond as an assistant.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
question: A labeler ranks K = 6 responses. How many pairwise comparisons does that give, and how many gradient terms does each single response appear in?
options: 6 pairs; each response appears in 1
30 pairs; each response appears in 10
36 pairs; each response appears in 6
15 pairs; each response appears in 5
explain: C(6,2) = 15 pairs, and each response is compared with the other K - 1 = 5. That correlation is why InstructGPT batches all pairs from one prompt together instead of shuffling them.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes
question: In the toy, which beta gives the best true quality among the ones shown, and why is the smallest beta not best?
options: beta = 1, because past it the policy shifts mass to the response the reward model overrates
beta = 0.1, because it has the highest reward model score
beta = 100, because any change from SFT hurts
All are equal, because the reward model is unbiased on average
explain: True quality is 0.27 at beta = 1 versus 0.24 at 0.5 and -0.38 at 0.1. Small beta lets the policy concentrate on Flattery, which the reward model overrates. Some optimization helps: beta = 100 leaves quality at 0.10.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
question: A term occurs in all N documents of the collection. How much does it contribute to any TF-IDF score using idf = log(N/df)?
options: Nothing, because its idf is log(1) = 0
A lot, because it has the highest tf
It depends on the base of the logarithm
It contributes its raw tf
explain: N/df = 1 and log(1) = 0 in every base, so the term has zero weight whatever its tf. idf turns such terms into automatic stop words for scoring, which is why the in our example stops dominating.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
question: Your build prints "undefined reference to `area'". `main.c` already has `#include "square.h"`, which declares `area`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add another #include "square.h" to area.c
Pass area.c (or area.o) to the link command
Compile main.c with -O2 so the call is inlined
Add the -E flag so the macro is expanded
explain: This message comes from the linker: main.o refers to the symbol area but no object file or library on the command line defines it. Headers only declare. -O2 (optimization level 2) cannot help: the compiler can only inline a body it can see, and main.c never sees area.c. The fix is to give the linker the definition, for example `gcc main.c area.c -o app`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
question: `unsigned char a = 250, b = 10; int s = a + b;` What is s?
options: Undefined behavior, because the sum overflows unsigned char
explain: Integer promotion converts a and b to int before adding, so the sum is computed as int and 260 fits. It would become 4 only if stored back into an unsigned char (260 modulo 256).

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
options: It tests errno instead of f: errno may be nonzero even though fopen succeeded
Nothing; errno is 0 whenever fopen succeeds
perror needs errno passed as an argument
fopen never sets errno, so the check never fires
